newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt to outline plans ahead of protests.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt to outline plans ahead of protests.

text.p: The Russian government is to explain on Wednesday how its new young team plans to tackle the nation's profound economic troubles. But good intentions are unlikely to deflect millions from staging protests the following day.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin will hand President Boris Yeltsin his proposals for remaining posts in a lengthy cabinet reshuffle and hold a news conference with his youthful new first deputies Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.

Trades union leaders have said, however, that they still expect as many as 20 million Russians to join strikes and protests on Thursday to show their discontent with the economy and especially with huge backlogs in wage and pension payments.

Yeltsin demanded drastic changes in the government earlier this month. Returning to active politics after eight months of illness, the 66-year-old Kremlin leader acknowledged that his market reforms were failing to meet people's needs.

In an effort to halt the decline in incomes and free the economy from a web of corruption, organised crime and Soviet-style bureaucracy, he parachuted in his 41-year-old chief-of-staff Chubais to spearhead a new wave of reforms.

Last week, in an apparent effort to break a deadlock between Chubais and the more conservative Chernomyrdin, he also named Nemtsov, 37, a liberal regional governor, as a first deputy prime minister with a brief to crack down on selfish monopolists.

After a week of foreign policy, including his summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton and meetings on Tuesday with Indian and Chinese leaders, Yeltsin convenes the Chernomyrdin-Chubais- Nemtsov troika on Wednesday to chart the way forward.

In a public show of concern ahead of the protests, the president on Tuesday ordered the government to do more to end wage delays and to help millions of investors who lost their savings in dubious investment schemes. He announced a fund to help war veterans and pensioners deal with their problems.
"I consider the situation with the mass delays in wage payments unbearable," Yeltsin was quoted as saying by his press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky.
Workers are owed over 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) in back wages, of which the state owes 10 trillion.
Government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said officials were working intensively to address trade union demands.
"In the last two weeks, large parts of the government have worked round-the-clock in connection with the reorganisation of the government and the union protests on March 27," he said.
Russia cannot immediately pay off its debts, but it can detail its approach to the problem.

"I wouldn't expect any revolutionary decisions in the next three to five days, two weeks, or even month on issues such as natural monopolies, social issues or other problems," Shabdurasulov told reporters.
"It's not real to imagine solving such a series of problems tomorrow or the day after tomorrow."
Back pensions would be paid by the end of June, debts to teachers by May, and government debts by the autumn.
It remained unclear to what extent Thursday's day-long protest would succeed, but Shabdurasulov said a small number of groups were ready to mar the event with violence.
Organisers said they had taken special security measures to maintain order. Previous efforts at organised protest have often failed to rally much support.
